editorNote: Late April 1983 put arcade trade papers, IBM PC business software, and discount home-computer shelves in the same weekend conversation, while the Beirut embassy bombing gave the week a stark world-news backdrop.
morningLine: This week at the counter: Pole Position still drives arcade chatter, Lotus 1-2-3 sells the IBM PC as an office machine, Flashdance takes the weekend box office, and Come On Eileen tops the singles chart.

lead.headline: Pole Position keeps arcade racing in the fast lane
lead.dek: Atari/Namco racing cabinets remained a trade-paper and operator touchstone as home-computer aisles tried to borrow arcade excitement.
lead.body: By the week of April 18, arcade operators were still talking about the drawing power of Pole Position, the Namco racer Atari distributed in North America. Its sit-down cabinet, qualifying lap, and billboard-style track made it a showroom example of how arcade spectacle could sell a game before a player touched the wheel. For home-computer buyers, that arcade glow mattered: software shelves were filling with conversions and racing titles that promised a slice of the coin-op floor.
lead.confidence: High for Pole Position release context; medium for week-specific retail emphasis.

computerItems.title: Lotus 1-2-3 defines the IBM PC pitch
computerItems.summary: Lotus 1-2-3, released earlier in 1983, was already becoming the spreadsheet/database/graphics package dealers used to explain why an IBM PC belonged on an office desk.

computerItems.title: IBM PC XT keeps fixed disks in the premium tier
computerItems.summary: The IBM Personal Computer XT, introduced in March 1983 with a 10 MB fixed disk, kept serious storage expensive but made hard-disk office computing easier to demonstrate.

computerItems.title: Home-computer game shelves stay crowded
computerItems.summary: Commodore 64, Atari 8-bit, Apple II, and TI-99/4A buyers saw arcade conversions, cartridges, and budget software competing for attention in 1983 dealer ads.

computerItems.title: Bulletin-board curiosity grows at 300 baud
computerItems.summary: Modems remained add-ons for enthusiasts, but the idea of dialing local boards and swapping files was becoming part of the hobby-computer sales pitch.

market.headline: Software is the margin story
market.summary: As home-computer prices fell and IBM PC systems grew more expensive with disks and monitors, dealers watched software, cartridges, printers, and support carry the profit conversation.

worldAnchor.headline: Bomb destroys U.S. Embassy in Beirut
worldAnchor.summary: On April 18, 1983, a truck bomb devastated the U.S. Embassy in Beirut, killing dozens and bringing Lebanon’s civil war and U.S. presence there to the front pages.

items.claim: Issue date follows Chronicle state file next_start_date=1983-04-18.
Pole Position was developed by Namco and distributed by Atari in North America, becoming a major 1982-83 arcade racing title.
Lotus 1-2-3 was released in 1983 and became a defining IBM PC business application.
IBM introduced the PC XT in March 1983 with a 10 MB hard disk and a roughly $4,995 list price.
Billboard Hot 100 for April 23, 1983 was led by Come On Eileen, with Mr. Roboto, Beat It, Der Kommissar, and Jeopardy in the top five.
Domestic weekend box office for April 22-24, 1983 was led by Flashdance, followed by Lone Wolf McQuade, Tootsie, Gandhi, and Monty Python's The Meaning of Life.
The U.S. Embassy bombing in Beirut occurred on April 18, 1983.
